summary: The narrator recounts to her companion, who is pondering in a thoughtful mood, her findings about Alex Goddard and Quetzal Manor, Colonel Ramos's threats against her and Carly over her film, and her belief that Ramos and his men roughed up Lou and took Sarah. The companion calls it a case of selling kids and suggests the Ninos del Mundo clinic is where Ramos took Sarah. He describes press reports of Americans attacked in Guatemala on suspicion of kidnapping Maya children for adoption, while the narrator insists the babies she saw at Quetzal Manor are not kidnapped Indian children. He warns about Guatemala's army and its 'disappeared' victims, and the passage ends with him referring to his pictures.
one_line: In Guatemala, the narrator tells her companion about Alex Goddard, Quetzal Manor, Colonel Ramos, and the suspicion that Sarah was taken for child selling.
key_facts: The narrator looked up at the canopy of stars, where the hunter and his sword dominated the sky like a stalwart centurion.
The narrator said, "I always know I'm in the tropics when it's right overhead."
The narrator told her companion about her findings on Alex Goddard and Quetzal Manor.
The narrator described how Colonel Ramos had threatened Carly and her about her film.
The narrator believed Colonel Ramos and a couple of his goons roughed up Lou and took Sarah.
The companion said the situation sounded like a classic case of selling kids, which he ranked with murder and grand larceny.
The narrator believed Alex Goddard's clinic was tied in with the situation, the place Sarah called Ninos del Mundo on her landing card.
The companion said there had been press stories over the last few years about Americans attacked in Guatemala on suspicion of trying to kidnap Maya children for adoption.
The companion said he had never seen proof of the kidnapping accusations and thought dumb gringos who misread the culture might be responsible.
The narrator said the babies she saw at Quetzal Manor were "Caucasian as vanilla snow cones" and not kidnapped Indian children.
The companion said that when a Guatemalan colonel is behind something, one should think twice about how many rocks to turn over.
The narrator said a man at the embassy named Barry Morton had said something similar to her.
The companion said Guatemala turned the word 'disappear' into a new kind of verb, with people 'disappeared.'
The companion said he knew some of the disappeared people back in the late eighties.
The companion described an Army truck rolling into a village at night, after which a few Maya were never heard from again.
